unit.unitTitle: The Power of Data: Using Data Modelling
unit.unitOverview:
Welcome to Unit 4. In this unit you will discover one of the most useful ideas in all of computing: using a computer to build a data model of a real-life situation. A data model is a way of representing something from the real world using data (words, numbers and dates) and the rules that link that data together. Once you have a good model, you can use it to answer questions, spot patterns and make sensible decisions.

You will do this with two kinds of free, open-source applications. The first is a spreadsheet called LibreOffice Calc, which organises data in rows and columns and carries out calculations using formulas. The second is a database application called LibreOffice Base, which organises data into tables of records and fields and lets you search it with queries. Both are part of LibreOffice, which you can download for free from libreoffice.org. Everything you learn here also works in similar tools, but the exact clicks and menu names in this unit are written for LibreOffice.

Because this course is self-paced, you are in control. You will read a little, then open the software and try it yourself, then check your work. By the end of the unit you will be able to model a real situation, calculate results automatically, store records safely, search them, and highlight the information that matters most.

concepts.title: Models and simulations
concepts.explanation:
A simulation is a more advanced kind of model. Simulations use a very large amount of data and often add realistic graphics so a person can see and interact with the situation. Training a pilot in a flight simulator is a good example: the trainee sits in a cockpit that looks and feels real and practises take-off and landing in different weather, with no danger to people or to an expensive aeroplane. Databases and spreadsheets build simpler models using words, numbers and formulae; simulations go further with complex graphics. Importantly, all the data behind a model or a simulation has to be stored somewhere — usually in a database.

Simulations have advantages and disadvantages. They can prevent loss of life during training, allow many different situations to be tried, and are usually cheaper and safer than using real equipment. On the other hand, they can be expensive to produce, and no simulation can include every possible factor, so the results are never a perfect match for reality.

concepts.title: Where data models are used across industries
concepts.explanation:
Data models and simulations appear in almost every industry. Here are the ones you should be able to describe:

Medicine and healthcare: doctors collect data such as a patient's age, symptoms and medication, then use specialised databases to help diagnose illness and choose treatment quickly.

Training: pilots, drivers and surgeons practise in simulators that behave like the real thing, so mistakes cost nothing and no one is harmed.

Scientific experiments: scientists model dangerous or slow processes — such as how temperature changes affect a reaction — to make predictions without real risk.

Weather and climate: forecasting models use data gathered from all over the world and from space, combined with complex formulae, to predict how weather patterns will change. This matters greatly for farmers in East Africa who plan around the Gu and Deyr rains.

Business: shops study sales data collected over years to spot patterns and predict demand, so they order the right amount of stock. A shop knows to store more bottled water before the hot season.

concepts.title: Spreadsheets: Modelling with LibreOffice Calc
concepts.explanation: Open LibreOffice Calc now. From the LibreOffice Start Centre, click Calc Spreadsheet, or open LibreOffice and choose File > New > Spreadsheet. You will see a grid. This grid is a worksheet, and it is divided into rows (numbered 1, 2, 3 …) and columns (lettered A, B, C …).

concepts.title: Cells and cell references
concepts.explanation:
Each box in the grid is a cell. A cell can hold text, a number or a formula. Every cell has an address made from its column letter and row number, called a cell reference. The cell where column B meets row 2 is cell B2. The cell where column D meets row 3 is cell D3. Click any cell and look at the Name Box on the left of the Formula Bar — it always shows the reference of the cell you have selected.

You can also select a group of cells called a cell range. A range is written as the first cell, a colon, then the last cell. So B2:B8 means every cell from B2 down to B8, and C2:E2 means C2, D2 and E2. The colon means 'through'. Ranges are how you tell a formula to work on many cells at once.

concepts.title: The Input Line and formulas
concepts.explanation:
Along the top of the window is the Formula Bar. The long white box in it is called the Input Line — this is where you type formulas. To enter a formula, click the cell where you want the answer to appear, type the formula, and press Enter.

Every formula must begin with an = sign. After the =, you can combine numbers, cell references and the arithmetic operators: + (add), — (subtract), * (multiply) and / (divide). For example, if B2 holds 10 and C2 holds 5, then typing =B2+C2 returns 15, and =B2*C2 returns 50. Using cell references instead of the raw numbers is powerful: if you later change B2, the answer updates by itself. That automatic updating is what turns a plain table into a living data model.

concepts.title: Worked Example 1 — SUM and AVERAGE (test scores)
concepts.explanation:
A function is a ready-made shortcut for a common calculation. The two you will use most are SUM (adds numbers) and AVERAGE (finds the mean). Type this small table into a new sheet, starting in cell A1:

Now click cell E2 and type =AVERAGE(B2:D2) then press Enter. Calc adds Nadia's three scores (8 + 7 + 9 = 24), divides by 3, and returns 8. Click E2 again, hover over the small square at the bottom-right corner (the fill handle), and drag down to E5 to copy the formula for every student. Sami's average becomes 7, Maya's becomes 9, and Leo's becomes 6.

There is more than one way to reach the same answer. Instead of the AVERAGE function you could type =(B2+C2+D2)/3, which also returns 8 for Nadia. The brackets matter: they make Calc add the three scores first and only then divide by 3. If you wanted the total instead of the average, you would use =SUM(B2:D2), which returns 24 for Nadia. Change the heading in E1 to 'Total' if you do this, so your labels always match your data.

concepts.title: Worked Example 2
concepts.explanation:
Data models are perfect for money. Imagine a small shop in Hargeisa records how much it sells each day for one week, in shillings. Enter this table starting at A1:

In cell B9 type =SUM(B2:B8) and press Enter. Calc adds all seven days and returns 700000 — the total sales for the week. In cell B10 type =AVERAGE(B2:B8); this returns 100000, the average daily sales. Notice how SUM and AVERAGE both work on the same range B2:B8 but answer different questions. If the shopkeeper had a great day and changed Friday's figure, both answers would recalculate instantly. This is the heart of a spreadsheet model: change one number and every linked result updates.

concepts.title: Formatting
concepts.explanation: A clear model separates the labels (headings) from the data. To make your headings stand out, select cells A1:C1, then press Ctrl+B or click the Bold button (the letter B) on the toolbar. To show money properly, select the sales figures, press Ctrl+1 to open Format Cells, choose the Numbers tab, then the Currency category, and pick a format. If Somali shillings is not in the list, choose the Number category with a thousands separator and keep the word 'shillings' in your column heading — the calculations work exactly the same either way.

concepts.title: Worked Example 3
concepts.explanation:
This is the most important idea in the whole spreadsheet section, so read it slowly. Your class is saving up for a trip to the ancient rock-art caves at Laas Geel. The trip costs a fixed 90,000 shillings per student. Each student pays over three months. Enter this table starting at A1, and type 90000 into cell H1 on its own:

First work out Total Paid. In cell E2 type =SUM(B2:D2) and press Enter; it returns 90000 for Nadia. Drag the fill handle from E2 down to E4. Because these are ordinary references, Calc helpfully changes them as it copies: E3 becomes =SUM(B3:D3) (returns 70000) and E4 becomes =SUM(B4:D4) (returns 70000). A reference that changes when copied is called a relative reference, and here it is exactly what we want.

Now the Balance, which is Trip Cost minus Total Paid. It is tempting to click cell F2 and type =H1-E2. For Nadia this returns 0 (90000 — 90000), which looks correct. But watch what happens when you drag the fill handle down: cell F3 becomes =H2-E3. There is nothing in H2, so Calc treats it as 0 and returns -70000 — a wrong, negative balance! The relative reference moved H1 down to H2, away from our trip cost.

The fix is an absolute reference. Change F2 to read =$H$1-E2. The dollar signs lock the reference to cell H1 so it can never move. Now drag the fill handle down again: F3 becomes =$H$1-E3 (returns 20000) and F4 becomes =$H$1-E4 (returns 20000). The H1 part stayed fixed while the E part moved, and every balance is correct. Remember the rule: use a relative reference when you want it to move, and an absolute reference (with $ signs) when it must always point to the same cell.

concepts.title: The fill handle
concepts.explanation: The fill handle is the small square at the bottom-right corner of a selected cell. When you hover over it the pointer becomes a thin cross; hold the mouse button and drag to copy a formula into neighbouring cells. A quicker way to copy a formula downward is to select the cell and the cells below it, then press Ctrl+D (Fill Down). This saves you from typing the same formula many times and is safe to use because relative references adjust automatically.

concepts.title: Conditional formatting
concepts.explanation:
Conditional formatting automatically changes how a cell looks when it meets a rule you set. Teacher Elena wants to see instantly which students have finished paying — that is, whose Balance equals 0. Select cells F2:F4, then choose Format > Conditional > Condition. Set the rule to Cell value is equal to 0, and under Apply Style choose Good (a green style) or click New Style to design your own. Click OK. Every zero balance now turns green, so a single glance tells the whole story.

You can add more than one rule. For the fair's money model you might want funds shown green when they reach the target and red when they fall short. If the funds total is in cell D6 and the target is in cell D8, you would set one condition 'Cell value is greater than or equal to $D$8 — Apply Style Good' and a second condition 'Cell value is less than $D$8 — Apply Style Bad'. Note that LibreOffice applies a cell style, not just a colour, which is slightly different from some other spreadsheets; the built-in Good and Bad styles are the quickest way to get green and red.

concepts.title: Charts
concepts.explanation: A chart turns numbers into a picture so patterns jump out. Suppose you have the approximate monthly rainfall for Mogadishu in one column of months and one column of millimetres. Select both columns including the headings, then choose Insert > Chart. The Chart Wizard opens. Choose Column as the chart type, click Next through the steps to add a title such as 'Mogadishu Rainfall (mm)', then click Finish and click outside the chart. You will clearly see the two rainy seasons — the Gu rains around April to June and the Deyr rains around October to December — far faster than by reading the raw numbers.

concepts.title: What-If and Goal Seek analysis
concepts.explanation: Because a model recalculates automatically, you can ask What-If questions simply by changing an input and watching the results. Change the trip cost in H1 and every balance updates at once. LibreOffice can also save different sets of inputs using Tools > Scenarios. A related tool works backwards: Goal Seek (under Tools > Goal Seek). You tell it the formula cell, the target value you want, and which input cell it may change, and Calc finds the input that reaches your goal. For the fair, Teacher Elena could use Goal Seek to answer 'what price must a T-shirt be so that total funds reach exactly 500,000 shillings?'

concepts.title: Databases: Modelling with LibreOffice Base
concepts.explanation: A database is best when your model is mostly about storing, organising and searching lists of things — like the competitors at the fair. Open LibreOffice Base. The Database Wizard appears. Choose Create a new database, keep the default embedded database, click Next, then Finish, and save the file with a name such as Fair.odb. You now have an empty database ready for tables.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

rules.text: A missing = sign is the number-one reason a formula does not work — Calc just shows your typing as text. If a whole column of copied results looks wrong, a reference probably needed $ signs to stay fixed. Database Terms Quick-Reference (LibreOffice Base)

terms: data
Raw facts and figures, for example a list of names or prices.
analyse
Examine something in detail so that you fully understand it.
data model
A computer representation of a real-life situation, where data is changed to see what happens.
simulation
A more complex model that can predict the outcome of a real-world system, often using graphics.
factors
The key data items represented in a data model.
spreadsheet
An application that uses rows and columns to organise data and carry out calculations (LibreOffice Calc).
database
An application used to organise data so it can be stored, processed and accessed electronically (LibreOffice Base).
cell
The box where a row and a column meet; it can hold text, a number or a formula.
cell reference
The letter-and-number address of a cell, for example B2.
cell range
A group of cells named by the first and last cell, for example B2:B8.
formula
A calculation you type into a cell; every formula begins with an = sign.
function
A built-in shortcut for a common calculation, for example SUM or AVERAGE.
relative reference
A reference that changes when a formula is copied, e.g. B2.
absolute reference
A reference that stays fixed when copied, written with $ signs, e.g. $H$1.
conditional formatting
Automatically formatting a cell that meets a specific rule.
field
A single piece of information in a database, shown as a column.
record
All the information about one item, shown as a row.
data type
The kind of data a field can store, for example text, number or date.
primary key
A field whose value is unique for every record, used to identify records.
query
A tool that searches a database and returns only the data you asked for.
criteria
The conditions a query uses to choose data, for example Age > 11.
